Participants performed a rapid target-pointing task where the offset between visual feedback and movement end-points was manipulated. This manipulation changed the expected location of the target relative to the actual hand movement. The visual feedback had horizontal offsets that varied based on the target's shape. Different shapes required different pointing adjustments to successfully hit the target. The target shapes were part of a continuous set, morphed between spiky and circular forms. This allowed researchers to test how people react to shapes that fall between the trained examples. After training, participants' performance was tested on novel target shapes, without feedback. Testing without feedback shows what the participants actually learned during the training phase. Learning the associations required explicit awareness of the cues' role, consistent with the Bayesian learning model. Participants applied the mapping of the trained shape most similar to the current one. The Bayesian learning model predicted that learning would slow down with more training pairs. Experimental results confirmed that increasing the number of shapes made the learning process slower. The good correspondence between the Bayesian learning model and empirical results suggests a possible mechanism for learning. This model explains how the brain manages simultaneously learning multiple visuomotor mappings.
